q: Which section of the CGST Act defines the scope of supply?
exp: Section 7 defines supply. Section 9 is the charging section and section 15 covers value.

q: For a transaction to be a supply under section 7(1)(a), it generally needs consideration and must be in the course or furtherance of business.
exp: Sale, transfer, barter, exchange, licence, rental, lease or disposal made for consideration in the course or furtherance of business. Schedule I lists exceptions where no consideration is needed.

q: Import of services for consideration by an individual for personal use is:
options: Not a supply as it's not in the course of business
A supply, even if not in the course of business
exp: Section 7(1)(b) makes import of services for consideration a supply 'whether or not in the course or furtherance of business'.

q: Barter (exchanging goods for goods) under GST is:
options: Not a supply as no money changes hands
A supply, both sides are supplies with consideration
exp: Consideration need not be money. In a barter, each party makes a supply to the other.

q: A company gifts a laptop worth ₹80,000 to an employee. It had claimed ITC on the laptop. Is this a supply?
options: Yes, gifts to employees above ₹50,000 in a year are treated as supply
Only if the employee pays something
exp: Schedule I para 2 covers supplies between related persons without consideration. Employer and employee are related, but gifts up to ₹50,000 per employee per year aren't treated as supply.

q: Stock transfer of goods from a company's Haryana GSTIN to its Punjab GSTIN (same PAN) is:
options: Not a supply as it's the same company
A supply even without consideration, since the two are distinct persons
A supply only if an invoice is raised
exp: Registrations of the same PAN in different states are distinct persons (s.25(4)). Schedule I makes supplies between them taxable even without consideration.
ref: CGST Act, s.25(4), Sch. I para 2

q: Which of these is treated as supply even without consideration?
options: Free samples given where no ITC was taken
Permanent transfer of business assets on which ITC was availed
Services of an employee to the employer
exp: Schedule I para 1: permanent transfer or disposal of business assets on which ITC has been availed.

q: A company in India imports services free of charge from its related entity in the US. This is a supply.
exp: Schedule I para 4 covers import of services by a person from a related person or from its own establishment outside India, in the course of business, even without consideration.

q: Services by an employee to the employer in the course of employment are:
options: Neither a supply of goods nor services
exp: Schedule III para 1. Salary is outside GST entirely.

q: Which of these is listed in Schedule III (neither goods nor services)?
options: Sale of a completed building after the completion certificate
exp: Sale of land, and of a building once the completion certificate is issued (or after first occupation), is in Schedule III. Under-construction flats are a taxable supply of services.
ref: CGST Act, Sch. III para 5; Sch. II para 5(b)

q: Goods are shipped from China directly to a buyer in the UAE, arranged and invoiced by a trader in Mumbai without the goods entering India. GST treatment?
options: Neither supply of goods nor services (merchant trade)
exp: Schedule III para 7 covers supply of goods from a place in a non-taxable territory to another non-taxable territory without the goods entering India.

q: High sea sales (goods sold by transferring documents before they cross customs) are:
options: Taxable at the time of each high sea sale
Neither supply of goods nor services; IGST is paid once at import
exp: Schedule III para 8(b). IGST is collected at the customs clearance stage instead.

q: Which actionable claim IS taxable under GST?
exp: Actionable claims are in Schedule III except specified ones: lottery, betting, gambling, horse racing, casinos and online money gaming.

q: Transactions in Schedule III count as exempt supplies for ITC reversal purposes.
exp: Mostly not. Schedule III items are outside supply. But the Explanation to s.17(3) specifically includes sale of land and sale of completed buildings as exempt value for ITC reversal. Most other Schedule III items are excluded.

q: A composite supply is taxed at:
options: The highest rate among the items
The rate of the principal supply
exp: A composite supply is naturally bundled and supplied together in the ordinary course of business, taxed at the principal supply's rate.

q: A Diwali gift pack of sweets, dry fruits and a chocolate box sold for one price is typically a:
exp: The items aren't naturally bundled; they're packed together for convenience. Mixed supplies are taxed at the highest rate among the items.

q: Goods sold with transport and insurance charged on the same invoice. How is it taxed?
options: Transport at 5%, insurance at 18%, goods at their rate
Everything at the rate applicable to the goods
exp: This is a classic composite supply with goods as the principal supply.

q: What primarily separates a composite supply from a mixed supply?
options: Whether the items are naturally bundled in the ordinary course of business
Whether one item is a service
exp: Both can have a single price. The test is natural bundling: would a normal buyer expect these together? If yes, composite; if they're just packaged together, mixed.

q: A hotel charges ₹6,000 per night for a room with breakfast included. How do you decide the rate, and what's the answer conceptually?
model: It's a composite supply because accommodation with breakfast is naturally bundled in the hotel business. Accommodation is the principal supply, so the whole ₹6,000 is taxed at the rate for hotel accommodation at that tariff, not split between room and food.
points: Single rate on the whole value, not split
exp: The Education Guide's illustration uses exactly this example.

q: A Gujarat supplier sells to a unit in a Gujarat SEZ. This is:
exp: Supplies to or by an SEZ unit or developer are treated as inter-state even within the same state.

q: Whether a supply is inter-state or intra-state depends on:
options: The locations of the supplier and the recipient
The location of the supplier and the place of supply
exp: Compare the supplier's location with the place of supply. Same state is intra-state; different states is inter-state.

q: Supplies to a foreign tourist in India who will take the goods abroad are treated as inter-state.
exp: Supplies to international tourists are deemed inter-state under s.7(5)(c) IGST.

q: Which of these is a 'non-taxable supply' under GST?
options: Supply of alcoholic liquor for human consumption
exp: A non-taxable supply is one not leviable to tax under the Act. Exempt supply includes nil-rated, wholly exempt and non-taxable.

q: Deemed exports under section 147 apply to:
exp: Deemed exports are notified supplies of goods manufactured in India that don't leave India, like supplies to EOUs or against Advance Authorisation.

q: An exempt supply includes:
options: Nil-rated, wholly exempt and non-taxable supplies
exp: The definition is wide. Zero-rated supplies are separate and are not exempt.

q: A client company gives its dealers free gold coins worth ₹20,000 each as a sales incentive. ITC on the coins?
options: Blocked, goods disposed of by way of gift
Available as a sales promotion expense
exp: The ₹50,000 employee gift limit doesn't apply to dealers, and 17(5)(h) blocks ITC on gifts.
